newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Sterling still hampering physical cocoa - trade.
newsitem.headline: Sterling still hampering physical cocoa - trade.

text.p: The slide in London-traded cooca futures has had scant effect on a quiet physical market in Europe as sterling's continued strength has negated much of the benefit for most consumers, traders said.

Physical buyers for products and beans came into the market and bought early last week when the combination of low futures and a slightly weaker sterling rate proved too tempting, but the currency's renewed rally since has stifled business once again.
Cocoa futures are trading around eight-month lows, with the benchmark March ending Tuesday at 913 stg a tonne. Scattered industry buying is one of the reasons the market has remained depressed.
"There's no sign the European consumer is following the market lower and if you add that to the fresh fund selling then you can see what's happened to the price," one trader said.

The lack of industry participation over the past couple of months continues to baffle some in the European trade. Some are now suggesting a possible link with the well-pubicised summer futures play which revolved around a squeeze on September.
"I don't know if they (industry buyers) are acting together or just all thinking in the same way," one said. "But it's almost as though the industry is on strike."
He said the avoidance of the physical market might be a ploy to force the hand of the major player involved in the squeeze, believed to be sitting on around 300,000 tonnes of cocoa.
"If you stay out of the physical side and just buy the term, the one holding the spot cocoa becomes the short," he said. "This may be a way of forcing that cocoa out."

Cocoa was continuing to arrive in Amsterdam, although tonnages were not large. Traders said the shipping situation in the Ivory Coast remained unclear and problems over shipping rates had held up some exports.
Ivorian Agriculture Minister Kouassi Konan said last week that marketing and freight rates for the 1996/97 season had been finalised.
But Amsterdam traders said although payments to farmers had been agreed, the freight side was still up in the air.
"The problem is with the cif side. There are rumours the Caisse wants to bring these freight rates down and that's holding things up," one trader said.
A few vessels were getting through to Amsterdam but the large bulk shipments would be a few more weeks, they said.

Arrivals in Abidjan were pegged by the trade at around 165,000 tonnes by November 10, roughly the same as last year. An arrival figure of around 250,000 tonnes by the end of November should confirm a main crop in excess of 900,000 tonnes.
